item.title: Claude Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2 Lead New Wave of Frontier AI Models
item.description:
Claude Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2 Lead New Wave of Frontier AI Models

🎉 One Year Later: Claude Opus 4.5 Anniversary

Today, November 24th 2026, marks the one year anniversary of the release of Claude Opus 4.5.

🧪 Testing Breakthroughs

  • Claude Opus 4.5 handles ambiguity and reasons about tradeoffs without hand-holding.
  • When pointed at a complex, multi-system bug, Opus 4.5 figures out the fix.
  • Tasks that were near-impossible for Sonnet 4.5 just a few weeks ago are now within reach.
  • Opus 4.5 was the first model I had used with Claude Code where the default result was generally the right thing.

⚙️ Claude Code Evolution

  • Claude Code was 9 months old at that point, having been introduced alongside Claude 3.7 Sonnet on February 24th, 2025.

📸 OpenAI’s GPT-5.1 Family

  • In November, OpenAI released GPT-5.1 Instant, GPT-5.1 Thinking, GPT-5.1-Codex, and GPT-5.1-Codex-Max.
  • These had a similar effect on their Codex coding agent: it became reliably useful for many of my coding tasks.

🔐 Claude Fable: Cybersecurity Breakthrough

  • We got our first hint of Claude Fable in April, when Anthropic announced Claude Mythos and said that it was too dangerous to release, due to its improved cybersecurity capabilities.
  • Mythos was a model that could not just find security vulnerabilities, but it could also figure out how to exploit them.
  • In June we got to see how good that model was for ourselves, with the release of Claude Fable 5—a defanged Mythos, that would solve most problems but would actively block you from using it for security work.
  • After three glorious days… the US government took it away from us.
  • Fable 5 was placed under export controls that effectively banned the model.
  • We wouldn’t get it back until July 1st.

🛠️ Revolutionary Automation

  • In June I wrote about how Claude Fable is relentlessly proactive, after I asked it to help fix a display glitch in Safari and it spun up its own pyobjc-framework-Quartz screenshot mechanism and a CORS-enabled localhost logging server to help resolve the bug.
  • A more recent example of the power of Fable class models is my mysterious beep finder from a couple of weeks ago.
  • I gave Opus 5.5 and then Fable 5.2 access to five WebAudio microphones in a room full of boxes and it was able to triangulate the source of an infuriating mysterious beep to within about 40cm.

🎮 3D Modeling Renaissance

  • I’d currently class Claude Fable 5, 5.1, 5.2 and Claude Opus 5.5 as Fable class (I think of Opus 5.5 as “cheap Fable”).
  • GPT-6 Astra got there for me too, and I think the new Gemini 4 Neon may count as well.
  • Something interesting happened with frontier LLMs over just the past four months: they got really good at 3D modeling.
  • I first noticed this with Claude Fable 5, but it really kicked into gear with Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and most recently the Gemini 4 family.

🎲 Game Development Breakthrough

  • Back in August I experimented with having Fable 5 build me a raccoon heist game.
  • It had 3D graphics, looked like a game, and played really poorly.
  • GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra did a much better job but the game itself was still pretty dull after the first 90 seconds of play.
  • I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 “This game isn’t fun enough yet. Make it a LOT more fun.”
  • My Command & Conquer-style RTS went from boring to deeply entertaining overnight, after Opus spent 12 hours playtesting new features and rebalancing the gameplay.
  • Opus 5.5 came out on September 22nd, 2026.

⚔️ Indie Games Culture War

  • The indie games scene has descended into a full-blown culture war over AI-assisted programming.

🖼️ Fable Class Capabilities

|| Model | Attributes || | — | — | | Claude Opus 4.5 | Handles ambiguity, reasons about tradeoffs without hand-holding | | Opus 4.5 + Claude Code | Default result generally the right thing | | Claude Mythos | Too dangerous to release due to improved cybersecurity capabilities | | Claude Fable 5 | Defanged Mythos, blocks security work | | Claude Fable 5.2 | Triangated beep source to within 40cm | | Claude Opus 5.5 | 12-hour playtesting, rebalancing gameplay, “cheap Fable” |

item.title: GPT-6 Designs Proteins Using Reasoning and Code
item.description:
GPT-6 Designs Proteins Using Reasoning and Code

OpenAI has demonstrated that its GPT-6 family of models can design new protein shapes and amino acid sequences using only reasoning and code, eliminating the need for specialized biology models to generate designs.

🔍 Overview

The development is detailed in a preprint titled “GPT-6 as a Universal Foundation Model for Protein Biology: Beyond Specialized Models.” This work shows that GPT-6 possesses intrinsic capabilities for designing new proteins, allowing it to generate structures and sequences without relying on external, specialized biology tools. The approach simplifies the workflow by using general-purpose coding and reasoning instead of coordinating multiple specialized models.

🧩 How it works

Proteins are chains of amino acids whose order determines their three-dimensional shape and function. GPT-6 models approach this by leveraging knowledge from math, physics, chemistry, and biology to reason about protein shapes and molecular interactions.

  • Prompting and Guidance: Researchers can guide designs by specifying where a protein should attach and what shape it should take. This allows for control ranging from a single bond between two atoms to the overall protein shape.
  • Task Flexibility: Models can switch between tasks—such as designing minibinders, building proteins around specific features, or predicting interactions—simply by changing the prompt, without requiring retraining.
  • Comparison to Specialized Models: While specialized models require substantial expertise and specific inputs, GPT-6 uses general-purpose coding. Internal tests showed that GPT-6 models performed comparably to or better than specialized models on most design tasks, although predicting a complete protein structure remained a clear weakness.

⚙️ Key details

Laboratory tests conducted with research partner Onava validated the computational designs.

  • Minibinder Design: For five target proteins, Onava created small proteins based on GPT-6.2’s 3D structures. In each case, at least one protein showed evidence of binding to its intended target.
  • Antibody and Minibinder Resequencing: GPT-6.2 designed new amino acid sequences for existing minibinders and antibodies. These redesigned molecules retained their binding capabilities in lab tests.
  • Ligand Docking: GPT-6.2 was asked to predict where and how a small molecule would bind to a protein, a task it accomplished by switching prompts without retraining.
Model Performance vs. Specialized Models (RFdiffusion)
GPT-6.2 Scored slightly lower on 3D design quality
Latest Internal Models Scored higher than specialized models

💡 Why it matters

Specialized biology models often have rigid input constraints and require changes to software or additional training to accept new types of information. GPT-6’s ability to handle diverse protein biology tasks through prompt changes and general reasoning suggests a more flexible approach to protein design. This capability allows researchers to guide designs with high fidelity, such as specifying the number of coils or strands in a minibinder, with internal models following such instructions with near-perfect fidelity in 3D designs.

#GPT-6 #ProteinDesign #OpenAI #Bioinformatics #AIResearch

Source: GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities

item.title: FineEnvs: An Open-Source Resource for End-to-End RL Environments
item.description:
FineEnvs: An Open-Source Resource for End-to-End RL Environments

A new open-source resource called FineEnvs has been released to address the shifting bottleneck in reinforcement learning (RL) for LLMs, where the environment design now poses a greater challenge than the algorithm. The project provides an end-to-end, reproducible, and open-source framework for designing, building, deploying, training against, and scaling RL environments to thousands of concurrent sessions.

🧩 How it works

The ecosystem is built on real, executable code rather than diagrams or unverified examples. Key characteristics of the resource include:

  • Reproducible Training: Every rollout has been executed, and every training curve comes from a job that users can launch in a single command without requiring their own GPU.
  • Comprehensive Coverage: The resource covers how to design an environment, how to build it, how to deploy it, how to train against it, and how to scale it to thousands of concurrent sessions.
  • Framework Agnosticism: The environments are compatible with six different frameworks, allowing users to train using SETA, native OpenCode, or Harbor, utilizing HF Jobs or Slurm.
  • Verified SFT Traces: Includes data-analysis tasks with verified SFT traces and a single-turn GRPO tutorial on HF Jobs.

⚙️ Key details

The release features three distinct environments demonstrated across six frameworks side by side. These environments utilize specific models and reward mechanisms:

Environment / Task Description Model / Reward Mechanism
Math Image OCR Train models to read math images into LaTeX Qwen3-VL-2B with a verifiable reward
Watercolour Painting Train models to paint watercolours by writing p5.brush sketches Qwen3.5-35B-A3B rewarded by an aesthetic preference model
VLM Navigation Drop a VLM at a random street corner on Earth Scored on kilometres of error
Document OCR & ASR OCR over a million pages in 22 languages and speech recognition over 102 Behind one OpenEnv server; Gemma 4 trained to read and hear Kannada
Port Logistics Re-plan a broken week of container-ship dockings at the Port of Barcelona Graded against a proven optimum; simulates live news, pilots, tugs, and real wind
JetBlue Operations Run JetBlue through a real storm day Two desks talk, then three with the passengers on board
Lean 4 Proofs OpenAI’s Comparator challenges as Harbor tasks Prove a research result in Lean 4, graded by Comparator in a separate sandbox
Math Proofs Write a natural-language proof of an olympiad problem LLM judge grades it 0–7 against the problem’s rubric (QED-Nano recipe)
24 Game Make the target from every card using + − × ÷ Variants include the current year from eight cards and any four-digit number from nine

🚀 Availability

The resource is accessible through the following locations:

  • Source, recipes, and notebooks: Available in the project repository.
  • Environments, datasets, models, and demos: Hosted at huggingface.co/FineEnvs.
  • Training Infrastructure: Supports execution via HF Jobs or Slurm.

item.title: Swarms-rs: First Enterprise-Grade Multi-Agent Orchestration Framework in Rust
item.description:
Swarms-rs: First Enterprise-Grade Multi-Agent Orchestration Framework in Rust

Swarms-rs has launched as the first-ever enterprise-grade, production-ready multi-agent orchestration framework built in Rust. The framework is designed to handle demanding tasks with unparalleled speed and efficiency, leveraging Rust’s performance and safety features to provide a scalable solution for multi-agent systems.

🔍 Overview

An agent in Swarms-rs is defined as an entity powered by an LLM equipped with tools and memory that can run autonomously to automate issues. The framework seamlessly manages and coordinates thousands of agents, allowing them to communicate and collaborate efficiently to achieve complex goals.

⚙️ Key Details

Key features and capabilities include:

  • Built with Rust’s zero-cost abstractions and fearless concurrency for optimal resource use
  • Near-zero latency and lightning-fast execution, ideal for high-frequency and real-time applications
  • Memory safety guaranteed through Rust’s ownership model, eliminating data races and memory leaks
  • Minimal overhead with maximum throughput and efficiency
  • Highly modular design for easy extension and customization
  • Scales from a handful of agents to millions while maintaining top-tier performance
  • Designed for real-world deployment with robustness for mission-critical tasks

💻 Technical Requirements

To use Swarms-rs, the following are required:

Requirement Description
Rust (latest stable version recommended) Programming language runtime
Cargo package manager Rust’s package manager
LLM API key For OpenAI, DeepSeek, Anthropic, etc.
Dependencies Multiple crates including tokio, anyhow, dotenv, and others

🚀 Availability

Installation is straightforward:

  • Run cargo add swarms-rs
  • Add supporting packages: cargo add tokio --features full, cargo add anyhow dotenv, and others
  • Create a .env file in your project root with API credentials

📊 Why It Matters

Swarms-rs represents a significant advancement in multi-agent system orchestration, offering developers a robust, efficient, and scalable solution built on Rust’s proven track record of performance and safety. The framework’s ability to handle mission-critical tasks while maintaining efficiency under heavy loads makes it an attractive option for industries requiring reliable, high-performance agent-based systems.

item.title: New Dockerized React/FastAPI app replicates LLM Council for model comparison
item.description:
New Dockerized React/FastAPI app replicates LLM Council for model comparison

A new React/FastAPI application is available for comparing model answers, peer rankings, and a chairman’s synthesis, inspired by Andrej Karpathy’s LLM Council concept.

🧩 How it works

The application allows each conversation to select OpenRouter or Ollama, its specific models, system prompts, and an execution mode. It supports persistent conversations, attachments, and streaming with cancellation and partial-result recovery. Execution is handled through bounded and idempotent model runs, with runtime settings controlled by administrators.

⚙️ Key details

  • Dependencies: The project uses a committed uv.lock and frontend/package-lock.json to ensure reproducible dependencies.
  • TOON statistics: Token representation comparisons are provided, but these are explicitly not provider billing.
  • Ports: The backend is published loopback-only at http://127.0.0.1:8001, while the frontend is published on port 80.
  • Proxy Limits: The frontend nginx.conf and optional nginx/nginx.conf files both set client_max_body_size to 25m. A 20 MiB image becomes approximately 26.7 MiB in base64, which can successfully upload but receive a 413 error at the proxy. To support the full API image limit, the setting must be increased to 40m and the proxy layer rebuilt.
  • Resources: The backend container has a 1 GiB total memory limit in Compose. PDF workers on Linux can each have a 1 GiB virtual-memory ceiling, with two workers per API process.
  • Databases: Compose does not provision PostgreSQL or MySQL servers. Adding PostgreSQL requires exporting base runtime dependencies with --extra database and rebuilding the image. Finance and embeddings extras similarly require explicit image packaging.
  • Environments: Python 3.10+ is declared by the project, with CI and the backend image using 3.12. Node 20.19+ or 22.12+ is required by the locked Vite release; the frontend image uses Node 22, while CI tests Node 20.
  • Configuration: In Docker, keeping a specific build-time setting empty utilizes the same-origin nginx proxy. Changing this setting for built assets requires a rebuild.

🚀 Availability

Running the application requires a running Docker engine and current Docker Compose v2. The default backend Dockerfile exports base runtime dependencies only.

item.title: Programming Navigation Launches Open-Source AI Quiz WeChat Mini-Program
item.description:
Programming Navigation Launches Open-Source AI Quiz WeChat Mini-Program

Programming Navigation has launched a new open-source educational project: an AI quiz WeChat mini-program built on Taro, React, FastAPI, and DeepSeek. Developed by Programmer Yupi and the Programming Navigation team using Vibe Coding and OpenSpec methodologies, the project is designed to teach the full workflow of AI programming, from requirement analysis to deployment and release within the WeChat ecosystem.

🧩 Core Functionality

The mini-program supports three primary methods for generating quiz questions, allowing users to customize learning paths without relying on fixed question banks:

  • One-sentence topics: Users input a brief concept or description, and the AI generates a corresponding set of questions.
  • Private document RAG: Users can upload PDF, Word, Markdown, or plain text files. The backend parses, chunks, and vectorizes the text into a Chroma vector database to generate questions strictly based on the uploaded private knowledge.
  • Web search integration: For time-sensitive or cutting-edge topics, the system utilizes web search to ensure generated questions reflect the latest facts.

The interface supports single-choice, multiple-choice, and true/false questions. Upon submission, the system immediately highlights correct and incorrect options and provides concise explanations and knowledge point categorizations. After completing a set of questions, the system generates a personalized AI review report that includes a mastery score, a list of weak knowledge points, a three-sentence summary, and learning suggestions, along with experience points rewards.

⚙️ Technical Architecture

The project employs a front-end and back-end separated design:

  • Front-end: Built with Taro 4 and React 18, including TypeScript and Sass.
  • Back-end: Powered by Python 3.11+ and FastAPI, utilizing Pydantic v2 and Uvicorn.
  • AI Orchestration: Uses LangChain and LangGraph to manage large language models and retrieval logic. Specifically, a ReAct autonomous decision agent is built on LangGraph to determine search keywords and execution rounds for web queries.
  • Data & Storage: Uses MySQL with aiomysql for asynchronous connection pooling and Tencent Cloud COS for object storage.
  • AI Services: Integrates DeepSeek for question generation and reporting, Alibaba Cloud Bailian for embedding and text-to-image generation, and Tavily for web search.
  • Authentication: Implements silent login via WeChat jscode2session and JWT, while also supporting an optional login architecture that allows unregistered visitors to experience the core quiz process.
  • Deployment: The back-end is containerized with Docker and deployed to WeChat Cloud Hosting, completing necessary AI service category applications, ICP filings, and domain configurations.

💡 Educational Context

This repository serves as a hands-on teaching project for the Programming Navigation AI Quiz Learning Mini-Program course. The curriculum covers 6 major business modules and over 30 functional points, aiming to allow students to complete the full development cycle and gain resume-ready skills in less than a week. The course includes video tutorials, written notes, resume writing references, interview questions, and one-on-one Q&A services.

item.title: Tencent Launches WeKnora: An Open-Source LLM-Powered Knowledge Framework
item.description:
Tencent Launches WeKnora: An Open-Source LLM-Powered Knowledge Framework

Tencent has released WeKnora, an open-source, LLM-powered knowledge framework for enterprise document understanding, semantic retrieval and reasoning. It brings a team’s documents together so they can be searched, reasoned over and kept up to date. The framework combines RAG for lookups, an agent for multi-step tasks, and a wiki for knowledge organization, all operating on the same knowledge bases.

📚 Core Components

WeKnora integrates three main capabilities:

Component Description
RAG Answers you can check, with hybrid search, multimodal parsing and citations
Agent Tasks done with knowledge and tools, with multi-step reasoning, skills and sandbox, the local browser, MCP tools and memory
Wiki Documents organized into a wiki, with a knowledge graph and rollback

⚙️ Key Features

  • Skills installed from ClawHub / SkillHub / Git / ZIP run in session-persistent Docker / E2B / Cube sandboxes, with an interactive terminal and graphical desktop beside the chat
  • BrowserSkill extension allows the agent to operate the user’s own Chrome or Edge, and external MCP services (OAuth included) can be connected and enabled tool by tool
  • Cross-session long-term memory keeps the profile, preferences and facts a user has confirmed
  • Folder uploads preserve directory structure, and retrieval chunks can be edited, diffed and rolled back
  • Auto-sync from multiple platforms including Feishu wiki, Confluence, GitLab, Notion, and others
  • Supports 10+ document formats including PDF, Word, images, Excel and XMind
  • Q&A integrations with WeCom, Feishu, Slack, Telegram, and embed widgets for external websites
  • 30 built-in vendors supporting OpenAI, DeepSeek, Qwen, Zhipu, Gemini, and others
  • Multi-workspace RBAC with four roles, per-resource ownership, audit logs, and Langfuse tracing
  • All components support swappable LLMs, vector databases, and storage backends
  • Can be deployed locally or on private cloud to keep data in user’s own environment

🚀 Availability

WeKnora is available as open-source software under the MIT license. The current version is v0.9.0, with documentation accessible at docs.weknora.weixin.qq.com and the project hosted at github.com/Tencent/WeKnora.

item.title: LangForce updates VLA-Arena results and accepts to ICML 2026
item.description:
LangForce updates VLA-Arena results and accepts to ICML 2026

LangForce has released updated performance metrics on the VLA-Arena benchmark and received acceptance to ICML 2026. The framework addresses a specific pathology in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model training known as Information Collapse, where models degenerate into vision-only policies by ignoring language constraints.

🧩 How it works

LangForce tackles the Vision Shortcut problem by forcing models to ground actions in language rather than relying solely on visual observations. It employs a dual-branch architecture and Bayesian decomposition to optimize policies.

  • Bayesian Decomposition: The model explicitly estimates a vision-only prior $p(a \mid v)$ and a language-conditioned posterior $\pi(a \mid v, \ell)$.
  • Latent Action Queries: Learnable queries are used to decouple vision-only and language-conditioned action distributions.
  • Optimization Objective: The policy maximizes the conditional Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI) between actions and instructions, effectively penalizing vision shortcuts and rewarding language-grounded actions.

📊 Updated Performance

The team has updated LangForce results on VLA-Arena, achieving average success rates of:

Benchmark Level Success Rate
L0 84.2%
L1 38.8%
L2 24.1%

Additional experiments on SimplerEnv and RoboCasa demonstrated an 11.3% improvement on the out-of-distribution (OOD) SimplerEnv benchmark using the exact same datasets as baselines. This approach also helps prevent the catastrophic forgetting of general multimodal reasoning capabilities common in standard VLA fine-tuning.

🚀 Availability

Model weights and checkpoints are publicly accessible for researchers and developers:

  • Hugging Face Collection: LangForce checkpoints are available in the Hugging Face collection.
  • starVLA Integration: LangForce has been integrated into starVLA, allowing for direct end-to-end training and evaluation on benchmarks such as LIBERO, SimplerEnv, and RoboCasa.

item.title: Hugging Face introduces RL-trained harness adapters for improved LLM efficiency
item.description:
Hugging Face introduces RL-trained harness adapters for improved LLM efficiency

Hugging Face has introduced “harness adapters,” a method for adapting favorite models to specific agent harnesses using reinforcement learning (RL) to improve performance and cost efficiency. While base models generally target general performance, combining a model with a specific harness often leaves performance and efficiency on the table for targeted tasks. By training custom adapters on specific task distributions, developers can squeeze more capability out of existing models for their specific use cases.

🧩 How it works

The technique involves combining RL on a custom task distribution with the user’s favorite agent harness. This process yields more accurate and efficient models specifically for that target harness and task combination. The core mechanism is that models are not fully optimized for every harness and task; they are optimized for general performance. With RL, a custom harness adapter can be trained to optimize the model for the specific harness and task at hand.

In recent experiments, researchers froze the weights of the Qwen3.8-27B model and added a custom RL-trained LoRA adapter. This approach resulted in the model reasoning less, calling fewer tools, and performing better on the first attempt.

Model / Configuration Terminal-Bench 2.1 Score Avg Tokens per Task
Qwen3.8-27B (Base) 39% 2.9K
Qwen3.8-27B (with RL LoRA) 55% 1.5K

⚙️ Key details

To validate this approach on harder real-world software engineering tasks, the team trained one LoRA adapter for Qwen3.8-27B for each of three agent harnesses: Pi, Hermes Agent, and OpenCode. The RL training occurred inside the harness itself. Datasets, training, and agent rollouts were managed on the Hub in Jobs using TRL’s AsyncGRPOTrainer, OpenEnv, and harbor.

Key technical components of the recipe include:

  • Super Adapter: The three individual LoRAs were merged into a single “super adapter” that runs unchanged under all three harnesses.
  • Docker Images: Ready-to-use docker images for RL tasks are provided with target harnesses pre-installed. The final images use Pi 1.5.2, OpenCode 2.2.7, and Hermes Agent v0.22.6.
  • Custom Dataset Pipeline: A custom dataset for agentic coding was created using the Hub, OpenEnv, and Repo2RLEnv. This pipeline combines task retrieval from existing RL environments, task generation via Repo2RLEnv, and task validation with OpenEnv.
  • Task Sources:
    • SWE-smith injects bugs into real Python and Go repositories using LLM rewrites or mutations.
    • SWE-Gym (packaged as Harbor tasks in TaskTrove) converts real GitHub issues and merged fixes into tasks.
    • Tasksmith generates tasks from merged pull requests. In one instance, Tasksmith produced 24 valid tasks from 30 merged pull requests in 10 Python repositories.

Every task in the dataset passes an eligibility screen via openenv validate and a difficulty check against the base model. Each harness adapter beat the base model under its own harness on both performance and efficiency benchmarks.

🚀 Availability

All artifacts related to this work, including adapters, GGUFs, RL tasks, and the safeagents plugin, are browsable through a Hugging Face collection. A fully reusable recipe is shared so developers can reproduce these results on their own task, harness, and model combinations.

item.description:
RadixArk Releases DaisyRose-27B Model With RL Training on Long-Horizon Agent Tasks

RadixArk has released DaisyRose-27B, its first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using the Miles framework. The model was trained on 1,200 curated long-horizon agent tasks over 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs, achieving a Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 improvement from 5.6% to 12.0%.

🔍 Overview

  • First model release from RadixArk
  • Base: Qwen3.8-27B
  • Training method: Reinforcement learning via Miles (open-source RL framework)
  • Training scale: 1,200 tasks, sessions up to 1M tokens, 18 days, 144 H200 GPUs
  • License: Apache 2.0 checkpoints available

🧩 How It Works

Task Design

  • Tasks built in partnership with Eigent AI from a large pool covering machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields
  • Thousands of candidates filtered to ~1,200 final tasks using three criteria:
    • Each task targets a mistake the original Qwen3.8-27B makes
    • Tasks redesigned around those mistakes, difficulty adjusted until solve rate falls in a useful learning range
    • Each task requires several interdependent steps: the agent must reason, plan, and execute across a long job
  • Each attempt runs up to 1.5 hours in a sandbox with >100 tool calls and >256K output tokens
  • Tasks must reward actually solving the problem; every task reviewed alongside model attempts; flawed tasks fixed or removed

Training Backend (Miles)

  • Fully asynchronous mode: agent keeps working while model learns, neither waits for the other
  • 128 H200s run inference on agent tasks; 16 H200s run the trainer
  • After each step, updated model deployed to the 128 inference GPUs
  • Internal training backend built for agent training: each step learns from a handful of very long sessions (up to 1M tokens) folded into multiple trajectories via harness summarization

Sandbox Service

  • Built on open-source AgentENV project (RadixArk contributes fixes)
  • Mid-September to mid-November: ~944,000 sandboxes run, up to 1,566 concurrent
  • Service scaled from 1 to 12 machines
  • 10 upgrades shipped, nearly all while training was running
  • 99% sandbox creation success across 9 weeks; >99.95% since late October

⚙️ Key Details

Benchmark Results

Benchmark Qwen3.8-27B DaisyRose-27B
Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 5.6% 12.0%
  • DaisyRose-27B scores higher than original Qwen3.8-27B on every benchmark evaluated

  • Gains also on reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks

Model Architecture

  • Retains Qwen3.8-27B architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window
  • Longer training sessions use harness summarization to span multiple trajectories
  • Model thinks before answering by default; reasoning returned in reasoning_content, final answer in content

Training Efficiency

Metric RadixArk Backend Open-Source Trainer (Megatron)
Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) 37% 16%
Training cost reduction 57% less GPU time baseline
Throughput (tokens/sec across 144 GPUs) ~16,800 ~8,300

item.title: Amazon SageMaker AI introduces KV cache-aware routing
item.description:
Amazon SageMaker AI introduces KV cache-aware routing

Today, Amazon SageMaker AI introduces KV cache-aware routing (KV-aware routing), a new routing strategy for real-time endpoints. It uses the cache state that the model container reports to send each request to an instance that already holds a long cached match for its prompt and isn’t too busy.

🔍 Overview

KV-aware routing is designed for teams that serve large language models (LLMs) with multi-turn conversations, long shared prompts, or heavy load. It addresses limitations in the previously introduced prefix-aware routing, which infers where a prefix is cached from the request alone. Because prefix-aware routing hashes the start of the request, it cannot tell when an instance has evicted that cache. Consequently, if an instance evicts older KV cache entries when its GPU memory fills up, the router keeps sending matching requests there as if the cache were still warm. Additionally, in multi-turn chats, each turn adds to the history; while a request is shorter than the configured PrefixLength, every new turn changes the text the router hashes, so the next turn can land on a different instance than the one that cached the earlier turns.

🧩 How it works

A model keeps the work it did on a prompt in GPU memory, the KV cache, and skips that work when the same start reaches the same instance again. KV-aware routing operates through three main components:

  • Model Container Reporting: The model container reports what it has cached.
  • Managed Cache Index: SageMaker AI keeps a managed cache index of that state for the endpoint.
  • Endpoint Routing: The endpoint uses the index to choose an instance for each request.

When a request arrives, the endpoint tokenizes the prompt and looks up the tokens in the index. The index holds only pointers: one-way, truncated hashes of cached content, each mapped to the instance or inference component copy that holds it. It never stores prompts, token IDs, request payloads, or KV tensors. Because the index matches on tokens rather than a fixed number of bytes, a multi-turn history can match in full as it grows. If instance A holds the cached start of a conversation, the next turn of that conversation goes to A.

The endpoint picks among candidates by weighing how much of the prompt each one has cached against how busy it is. A candidate that is too busy is skipped, so if the instance with the longest match is busy, the request goes to the next-best one that is available. If no candidate has a useful match or all of them are busy, the request falls back to load-aware routing.

⚙️ Key details

You turn on KV-aware routing in two places:

  • Add one environment variable to your model so the container reports its cache contents.
  • Set RoutingStrategy to KV_AWARE in the endpoint configuration.

Specifically, when you turn events on with SM_VLLM_KV_EVENTS_CONFIG, the container publishes a KV cache event each time it stores or evicts cache entries, and SageMaker AI uses these events to keep the index current. Clients call the endpoint with the same APIs as before. You do not configure a concurrency threshold for this, as you do with prefix-aware routing.

💡 Why it matters

This strategy ensures that requests sharing a prompt are routed to instances where that prompt is already in the GPU memory cache, maximizing computational efficiency. By tracking actual cache eviction and storage events rather than relying on static prefix hashes, the system prevents routing requests to instances where the cache has been cleared due to memory pressure.

item.title: Five new developments in long-term AI memory and agent evolution
item.description:
Five new developments in long-term AI memory and agent evolution

Recent technical updates in artificial intelligence focus on improving how agents manage long-term memory, evolve their internal states, and handle stale data or corrupted inputs. These developments span architectural innovations for memory storage, learnable policies for memory transformation, governance strategies for conflicting facts, and the impact of data corruption on recall accuracy.

🔍 Overview of Memory Innovations

  • KV-LTM: A new memory tier stores raw session text plus the KV cache under a fixed reader model, answering queries by restoring cached sessions.
  • EvoDisco: Formulates agent memory evolution as evolutionary strategy discovery, allowing agents to learn which operators to apply rather than following a static schedule.
  • RegimeCouncil: An online router that arbitrates between local and global memory sharing scopes to manage stale facts without retraining the LLM.
  • Corrupted Memory Testing: A study testing whether intentionally corrupting training data prevents LLM agents from overfitting to recent events.

🧩 How It Works

KV-LTM Architecture This approach is complementary to retrieval and indexing. It treats text as the memory of record while using the cache as a recompute-free prefill accelerator. The design includes:

  • Storage records and budget-derived retention.
  • An append-only read path and bounded aggregation.
  • Analytical sizing where per-token state spans approximately 31K-328K bytes for pinned BF16 full-attention and latent-cached MLA configurations.
  • A per-user-year storage estimate of approximately 0.34-3.6 TB at a 30K-token/day scenario, compared to approximately 49 MB of raw text.

EvoDisco Policy A learnable policy conditions on current memory state and recent task history to select and instantiate one of four semantic operators:

Operator Function
Abstract Compress related memories
Refine Decompose overloaded entries
Bridge Connect weakly linked experiences
Reframe Reorganize retrieved reasoning chains

The policy updates via a bi-level fitness: an inner signal scores transformation quality, while an outer signal scores strategic efficacy over past decisions.

RegimeCouncil Governance This system addresses the “memory conflict governance” problem where stored facts go stale. It uses a paired-evidence router with three modules:

  • Local Advisor: Tracks the latest outcome on a queried fact alone.
  • Global Advisor: Pools recent outcomes across all stored facts.
  • Meta Governor: Defaults to the Local Advisor to avoid cross-fact interference but switches to the Global Advisor when global pooling shows a positive utility margin.

⚙️ Key Details and Results

  • KV-LTM Evaluation: Requires no persistent-cache implementation for logical QA evaluation. It uses per-session prefill to emulate valid cache reuse. System-level comparisons on LongMemEval indicate that commercial assistants often score below models reading history offline, consistent with content loss between write and read phases.
  • EvoDisco Performance: In a one-pass online plus frozen-transfer protocol on ALFWorld, WebShop, and LifelongAgentBench, EvoDisco outperforms strong memory baselines like MemP and MemRL. The largest gains are observed on ALFWorld, with improvements of +8.8 to +12.9 points over MemP and +16.4 to +17.9 points over MemRL.
  • RegimeCouncil Performance: Across LongMemEval update streams and historical drift tests on TempLAMA and TAQA, RegimeCouncil outperforms the better fixed-scope policy by 5.2-7.3 points on primary disagreement episodes. Ablations show that removing any of its three modules reduces accuracy by 2-7 points.
  • Dream Hypothesis Test: An agent using Claude Opus 5.5 stored learned information in text memory and rewrote it nightly from transcripts with 5-40% corruption. The results showed that corruption did not help the agent apply earlier learned tasks. Replacing details in 40% of turns lowered recall from 76% to 60%. Random-text corruption had no consistent effect because the model recognized it as corrupted and excluded it from memory.

💡 Why It Matters

These updates address critical inefficiencies in long-term AI interactions. KV-LTM trades storage for avoided re-prefill compute and write-time fidelity, solving the problem where personal assistants accumulate months of conversations but struggle with derivation and selection. EvoDisco moves beyond fixed memory operators, allowing agents to dynamically decide how to transform their memory based on strategic efficacy. RegimeCouncil provides a lightweight method to handle delayed feedback from stale facts without the complexity of full LLM retraining. Finally, the corruption testing suggests that pretrained models can easily separate corrupted text from real events, implying that fair tests of memory evolution require learners that cannot make this distinction as easily, such as those fine-tuned on specific corrupted data or operating in invented worlds.

The same architecture drives real-time graph analytics for fraud detection, network analysis, infrastructure monitoring, and other operational workloads where performance matters. item.title: Study: LLM Thinking Effort Boosts Confidence, Not Accuracy in Shopping Agents
item.description:
Study: LLM Thinking Effort Boosts Confidence, Not Accuracy in Shopping Agents

Researchers benchmarked ten frontier large language models (LLMs) acting as autonomous shopping agents to test whether increased computational effort improves purchase decisions. The study found that while “thinking harder” significantly raised the models’ stated confidence, it did not improve the actual quality of their product choices.

🔍 Overview

The study investigates two questions regarding LLMs deployed as shopping agents: does asking a model to think harder make it choose better products, and does the confidence it reports accurately predict the likelihood of error? The work challenges the assumption that models with more thinking power inherently make higher-quality purchasing decisions.

🧩 How it works

The agents process multimodal product listings, utilizing both visual and text data, to recommend purchases on behalf of consumers. To evaluate this capability, the researchers benchmarked ten frontier models using three specific product-choice datasets:

  • WebShop: A general web shopping benchmark.
  • Amazon SQID: A platform dataset from Amazon.
  • Wayfair WANDS: A platform dataset from Wayfair.

⚙️ Key details

The results across all three benchmarks revealed several critical findings about model performance and reliability:

  • Confidence vs. Correctness: Increasing thinking effort raised stated confidence at a statistically significant level but did not increase decision quality in a statistically meaningful way.
  • Calibration: Most models were not well-calibrated at every effort level, meaning their reported confidence percentages did not match their true correctness percentages.
  • Shared Errors: Errors were strongly shared among models; when one model made an error in a task, several others tended to err on the same task.
  • Convergent Wrong Answers: On tasks where multiple models all made errors, a large number of them picked the same wrong product.

💡 Why it matters

This research highlights a divergence between the subjective assurance reported by LLMs and their objective decision-making accuracy in commercial contexts. It suggests that for autonomous shopping agents, additional computational resources may yield higher stated confidence without corresponding gains in correctness, which has implications for relying on these systems for financial or consumer decisions.

item.title: Amazon Bedrock Open-Weight Models Support Explicit Prompt Caching
item.description:
Amazon Bedrock Open-Weight Models Support Explicit Prompt Caching

Open-weight models on Amazon Bedrock now support explicit prompt caching. This update allows developers to reuse computed prompt prefixes across requests, reducing input costs and response latency by reading repeated context from cache instead of processing it again.

🔍 Overview

Prompt caching reuses the computed state of a matching prompt prefix. When a request starts with the same content as an earlier one, Amazon Bedrock reads that prefix from the cache and processes only the remainder. Cache reads are billed at a lower rate than standard input, meaning savings grow each time a prefix is reused. Depending on the model, cache writes can be billed at a higher rate than standard input, but Amazon Bedrock manages the cache automatically.

🧩 How it works

Developers can use implicit caching, which works automatically on a best-effort basis, or explicit caching, where specific reusable prefixes are marked.

  • Implicit Caching: Amazon Bedrock reuses eligible prefixes automatically. In a conversation, each request resends the full context, so the previous request becomes the cached prefix for the next one. As recommended by the prompt caching guide, static content should be placed first and dynamic content last to keep the start of the prompt stable. If an early part changes, the cache is rebuilt from that point.
  • Explicit Caching: Users mark the end of each reusable prefix with a cache breakpoint. Content up to each breakpoint is written to cache once and read on later requests, while content after the last breakpoint is processed on every request. Users can add several breakpoints, up to the model’s maximum, to cache layers that change at different rates. This method limits cache writes to the shared prefix, preventing higher write-rate billing for content that is never read back on models that charge for cache writes.

On the Chat Completions API, explicit caching is configured using prompt_cache_options with the mode set to explicit, plus one or more prompt_cache_breakpoint markers.

⚙️ Key details

Feature Detail
Caching Modes Implicit (automatic) and Explicit (user-marked)
Data Privacy Prompts and outputs are not shared with the model provider or used to train models
Configuration Use prompt_cache_breakpoint markers on the Chat Completions API
TTL Time to live resets with each cache hit; specific durations vary by model
Minimums Minimum token count and maximum breakpoints vary by model; check the model card

Amazon Bedrock checks the prompt cache for a matching prefix, reads a matching prefix from cache, and writes new cacheable content to cache.

🚀 Availability

Amazon Bedrock manages the cache for you. Model availability and prompt caching support vary by AWS Region. An AWS account with access to the selected model on Amazon Bedrock is required. Developers should check the model card for the Regions that the model supports, as well as specific caching modes, minimum prefix lengths, and entry retention times.

Requests are sent to the Amazon Bedrock Runtime endpoint in your selected Region, authenticated with a short-term Amazon Bedrock API key.

item.title: Higher-Order Expert Pruning (HOPE) Improves Memory Efficiency in Large MoE Models
item.description:
Higher-Order Expert Pruning (HOPE) Improves Memory Efficiency in Large MoE Models

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have enabled state-of-the‑art LLMs to be scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but they come with a fundamental and costly caveat: every expert MLP must occupy memory at inference time, even though the vast majority are idle for any given token.

🔍 Overview

  • Expert pruning is one of the most direct fixes to this memory bottleneck.
  • Pruning avoids the latency issues which make dynamic loading/off-loading of experts impractical; it does not require any training; and it composes with quantization.
  • Existing pruning methods score each expert independently, assigning every expert a scalar importance score (based on a calibration dataset), and cutting out the least important experts (in each layer independently). These are first‑order methods because they assume each expert’s contribution is independent of all others.
  • Our newest paper derives HOPE (Higher‑Order Pruning of Experts), a second‑order method that accounts for pairwise expert interactions.

🧩 How MoE Routing Works

  • In a standard MoE, each layer has experts, and each input token is routed independently to such experts.
  • Routing is performed by a single layer which produces softmax‑normalized gate weights for each expert, wherein the experts with the highest gate weights are selected to form the active set of experts.
  • Expert co‑selection patterns emerge early in training and stabilize throughout.

⚙️ Memory Bottleneck Example

Model Experts per Layer MoE Layers Experts Used per Token Parameter Memory (≈) % Memory Used by Experts
Qwen3.5‑122B 256 48 8 250 GB 95 %

✂️ First‑Order Pruning Limitations

  • Ignoring expert interactions leads to suboptimal pruning, especially at aggressive rates.
  • Removing expert A might seem fine on its own, but if expert B— which frequently cooperates with and relies on A — is highly important, then removing A would dismantle a cooperative group just through a single deletion.
  • First‑order methods miss this entirely, because they score A and B separately.

📈 HOPE Method Details

  • When we delete a set of experts from some MoE layer, the selected set of experts for any token can change. The resulting change in layer output is the pruning error.
  • HOPE defines a tractable surrogate that strictly upper‑bounds the dominant component of the pruning error.
  • The surrogate leads to a quadratic program (QP): the F‑matrix is collected on the calibration dataset, where each entry captures the average gate‑weighted output product of experts i and j across tokens where both are co‑activated.
  • Diagonal entries measure individual expert importance; off‑diagonal entries measure pairwise cooperative contribution.
  • The QP is solved with a continuous relaxation and then rounded to binary solutions to obtain the optimal prune‑set.

🚀 Results

  • At 50 % pruning, HOPE achieves the best average rank of any method, with gains of up to +6.1 % on agentic coding tasks over the next‑best pruning method.
  • Removing up to 50 % of experts risks breaking many cooperative links; this is where second‑order pruning is most advantageous.

📊 Visual Insights

  • Visualization of the interaction matrix F for GLM‑4.5‑Air (128 experts per layer, 106 B parameters total) shows block structure after clustering experts, illustrating stable cooperative groups across early, middle, and late layers.

All statements are drawn from the cited evidence.

Source: Your Experts Have Partners. There’s HOPE for Keeping Them Together

item.title: FlexFloor Enables Faster Reinforcement Learning Post‑Training for Large Language Models
item.description:
FlexFloor Enables Faster Reinforcement Learning Post‑Training for Large Language Models

FlexFloor is a system that reduces the compute bottleneck of reinforcement‑learning (RL) post‑training for large language models by releasing resources earlier during synchronous response generation.

🔍 Overview

  • RL post‑training improves the capabilities of large language models, but generating training responses consumes most of the compute.
  • In mixture‑of‑experts models, workers that finish generating their assigned responses often stay occupied because their experts are still needed by other workers processing longer responses.
  • About one‑third of occupied worker time in the baseline occurs after the local response generation has already finished.

🧩 How it works

  • FlexFloor jointly adapts response scheduling and the active group of workers.
  • It leverages historical response lengths and memory constraints to decide how to batch prompts and where to place them.

item.title: Sparse Autoencoders Reveal How LLMs Encode Grammatical Number
item.description:
Sparse Autoencoders Reveal How LLMs Encode Grammatical Number

Large Language Models (LLMs) can be probed with Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to expose how they represent grammatical number. Researchers trained SAEs on a 70‑million‑parameter model (Pythia‑70M) and showed how specific SAE‑derived features drive the model’s choice of plural versus singular verb forms.

🔍 Overview

  • SAEs translate LLM hidden‑state vectors into a human‑comprehensible list of features or symbols.
  • They provide insight into an LLM’s knowledge representation and internal “mental” grammar, which is of pragmatic interest for mechanistic interpretation of AI behavior.

🧩 How it works

  • An SAE was trained on the hidden states of Pythia‑70M, a model with fewer than 100 M parameters trained on a small corpus.
  • The SAE discovered features named “plural noun”, “plural matrix subject”, and “generate a plural verb”.
  • By adding or removing these features from the hidden states of tokens, the researchers observed changes in the verb form the model generated.

⚙️ Key Findings

  • Adding the plural features causes the model to produce plural verbs such as are, do, or have in responses to prompts like “the men in the park”.
  • Removing those features from plural‑subject noun tokens makes the model produce singular verbs (is, does, has) instead.
  • Corresponding “singular noun” and “generate a singular verb” features are not as effective for forcing singular verb forms.
  • This asymmetry suggests that Pythia‑70M uses a privative representation of grammatical number in English.
  • The same approach replicated on larger models (Gemma‑2‑2b and Llama‑3.1‑8b) yielded similar results.

Feature Effect on Verb Form
plural noun Promotes plural verb generation
plural matrix subject Promotes plural verb generation
generate a plural verb Promotes plural verb generation
singular noun Less effective at inducing singular verbs
generate a singular verb Less effective at inducing singular verbs

💡 Why it matters

  • Shows a concrete mechanism for probing and steering LLM grammar via SAE‑derived features.
  • Introduces a novel methodological contribution for mechanistic interpretation of AI behavior.

item.title: Parameter Labs uncovers account takeover exploit in ChatGPT HTML preview sandbox
item.description:
Parameter Labs uncovers account takeover exploit in ChatGPT HTML preview sandbox

Parameter Labs reported a previously unknown vulnerability that let an attacker take over a ChatGPT user’s account by abusing the HTML preview sandbox.

🔍 Overview

  • The flaw was found in ChatGPT’s implementation of the artifacts pattern, formerly called Canvas and now referred to as HTML previews.
  • Interactive custom HTML apps are displayed inside a sandboxed iframe to keep untrusted code isolated from OpenAI APIs and private user data.

🧩 How it works

  • OpenAI uses the MathLive JavaScript library for graph support; the library includes a virtual keyboard that can be triggered from the sandboxed iframe via postMessage().
  • The parent‑page code that receives these messages inserts the supplied content with innerHTML.
  • Because there is no guard preventing other sandboxed frames (including HTML preview frames) from calling this method, an attacker can inject arbitrary HTML.
  • While innerHTML does not run <script> elements directly, it can be used to add a new iframe that is not sandbox‑restricted.
  • OpenAI’s Content Security Policy (CSP) blocks inline scripts and only permits script loading from a short whitelist of domains; YouTube is on that list.
  • The YouTube oEmbed endpoint can reflect JavaScript back to the page, allowing the injected iframe to execute code.
  • With JavaScript execution inside the ChatGPT UI, an attacker can call OpenAI APIs, fetch private user data, and exfiltrate it through an image reference.
  • The final outcome is a crafted ChatGPT share URL that, when opened by another signed‑in user, can steal that user’s private data or act on their behalf.

⚙️ Key details

  • The vulnerability relied on a complex attack chain linking the MathLive postMessage, innerHTML injection, CSP whitelist, and YouTube oEmbed.
  • Exploiting the chain gave full JavaScript execution within the ChatGPT interface.
  • The exploit allowed account takeover via a simple share link.

🛡️ Mitigation

  • OpenAI patched the issue and closed the hole.
  • A $5,000 bug bounty was paid to the discoverer, which the reporter considered low given the severity.

#OpenAI #Security #ChatGPT #BugBounty

Source: How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts

item.title: Amazon SageMaker AI adds serverless training session APIs for custom model fine‑tuning
item.description:
Amazon SageMaker AI adds serverless training session APIs for custom model fine‑tuning

🔍 Overview

Amazon SageMaker AI has expanded its serverless model‑customization offering with the general‑availability launch of training sessions. The new APIs let customers write and coordinate their own post‑training logic—such as custom loss functions or reward signals—while SageMaker AI handles all GPU infrastructure, fault recovery, and checkpoint storage.

🧩 How it works

Training sessions expose low‑level operations (e.g., forward_backward(), optim_step(), sample()) as SageMaker API calls. Users write the training loop in their own Python process; each call is executed on a live, stateful GPU‑backed session. The service takes care of:

  • GPU allocation and distributed execution
  • Gradient synchronization and checkpoint storage
  • Fault recovery, tenant isolation, and scaling
  • Security configuration via IAM roles, optional KMS keys, and VPC settings

Your data, checkpoints, and any custom weights stay in your Amazon S3 bucket in the region you choose, and SageMaker does not reuse them to train other models.

⚙️ Key Features

  • No instance‑type or cluster management – the service automatically provisions serverless GPUs.
  • Fine‑grained algorithmic control – write custom loss, reward, or preference functions.
  • Multi‑turn reinforcement learning – managed, serverless support for agents that require several interaction rounds.
  • Flexible adaptation – choose Low‑Rank Adaptation (LoRA) or full fine‑tuning, and chain techniques through continuous customization.
  • Pay‑per‑token pricing model.
  • Secure execution – IAM execution role, optional KMS key, VPC configuration, data stays in your S3 bucket.
  • Evaluation before deployment – built‑in steps for accuracy, bias, and safety checks.

📚 Programming Model

Training sessions are accessed through three SageMaker Python SDK clients:

  1. ServiceClient – sets platform‑level settings (execution role, model package, S3 output location, optional KMS/VPC) and starts a session.
  2. TrainingClient – provides operations such as forward(), forward_backward(), optim_step(), and checkpoint handling.
  3. SamplingClient – handles sample() and compute_logprobs() for generation and scoring during roll‑outs.

Each API call maps to a single step in your loop. An active session also exposes an OpenAI‑compatible chat completions endpoint, enabling existing client code to sample from the customized model.

🚀 Availability

The training‑session APIs are now generally available as part of SageMaker AI serverless model customization. A companion training sessions cookbook provides ready‑to‑run SFT and RL recipes.

💡 Why it matters

Customizing an open‑weight model with post‑training techniques such as reinforcement learning or preference optimization yields more accurate results for a specific business context (e.g., product catalogs, clinical vocabularies) and reduces inference cost. The new serverless APIs remove the operational burden of managing GPU clusters, allowing teams to focus on algorithmic innovation while still retaining full control over the training procedure.

item.title: Benchmarking Seven LLMs for Epilepsy MCQ Generation Reveals Strengths and Limits
item.description:
Benchmarking Seven LLMs for Epilepsy MCQ Generation Reveals Strengths and Limits

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate medical assessment items, but their reliability for disease‑specific question writing remains uncertain. A new benchmark evaluated seven publicly accessible LLMs on the task of creating single‑best‑answer epilepsy multiple‑choice questions (MCQs).

🔍 Overview

  • Purpose: Test how well current LLMs can draft epilepsy MCQs that meet educational standards.
  • Scope: Seven LLMs, 60 predefined tasks per model, total 420 generated questions.

⚙️ Benchmark Design

  • Prompt protocol: Identical single‑turn prompt for every model; no model‑specific tuning, web search, or external tools.
  • Task categories: Foundational knowledge, clinical cases, treatment decision‑making, diagnostic evaluation, longitudinal management.
  • Evaluation layers:
    • Objective metrics: structural compliance, keyed‑answer accuracy, textual characteristics, response time.
    • Expert review: Two blinded clinicians rated rigor, clarity, distractor quality, educational usefulness, cognitive alignment, and overall usability on five‑point scales.

📊 Results

  • Structural compliance: First‑pass compliance ranged from 83.33 % to 100 %; after one standardized corrective prompt, all 420 questions met structural requirements.
  • Keyed‑answer accuracy: Varied from 61.67 % to 98.33 %; Claude‑5 achieved the highest accuracy (98.33 %).
  • Composite expert scores (median):
    Model Composite Expert Score
    GPT‑5.6 3.75
    Claude‑5 3.67
    Kimi‑K3 3.50
  • Distractor quality: Median scores of only 2–3 across all models, indicating a common weakness.
  • Usability outcomes:
    • Directly usable without revision: 2 questions (0.48 %), both from GPT‑5.6.
    • Usable after minor revision: 119 questions (28.33 %).
    • Required substantial revision: 299 questions (71.19 %).
  • Additional observations:
    • Longer outputs correlated with better cognitive alignment but not with content rigor or clarity.
    • Response time showed no relationship to overall usability.

💡 Implications

  • Contemporary LLMs can reliably reproduce the structural format of epilepsy MCQs, yet structural compliance and answer accuracy alone do not guarantee educational readiness.
  • Weak distractor construction remains a major barrier to direct deployment.
  • LLMs may serve as assistants for expert‑supervised item drafting, but independent clinical review and subsequent learner‑based psychometric validation are still required before incorporation into medical education curricula.

item.title: Fused MoE Kernel Optimizes Decode Performance on NVIDIA Hopper GPUs
item.description:
Fused MoE Kernel Optimizes Decode Performance on NVIDIA Hopper GPUs

Mixture‑of‑Experts (MoE) models boost LLM capacity while keeping per‑token compute low, but the decode phase suffers from high latency because the underlying GPU kernels are inefficient.

🔍 Overview

  • MoE is a sparsely‑activated architecture that scales large language model capacity while keeping per‑token compute low.
  • MoE operations make up a large share of total compute time, so inefficiencies directly raise request latency and cost.
  • Optimizing MoE operations through kernel engineering offers the largest opportunity for performance gains.

🧩 How MoE and Fused Kernels Work

  • Fused MoE merges token routing, data shuffling, and specialized network calculations into a single batched GPU operation, replacing separate sequential loop operations.
  • This fusion provides latency advantages but adds complexity to kernel implementation and debugging.

⚙️ Hopper WGMMA Constraints

  • NVIDIA Hopper uses the Warp Group Matrix Multiply‑Accumulate (WGMMA) instruction, executed across a cooperative warp‑group of 128 threads.
  • In the wgmma.mma_async definition, the hardware fixes the matrix row dimension M to 64, defining the thread‑mapping topology.
  • Operand A must occupy this fixed M = 64 dimension (using registers or shared memory); Operand B occupies the variable N dimension via a shared‑memory descriptor.
  • The operand slots are structurally non‑interchangeable, and peak tile utilization requires M ≥ 64.
  • The hardware enforces a minimum layout shape for the leading dimension of the first operand, locking the block height to exactly 64 rows.

Table: Operand Mapping on Hopper WGMMA

Operand Fixed/Variable Dimension Mapping Requirement
A Fixed M = 64 rows Must fill a 64‑row layout bucket
B Variable N dimension Can be large (e.g., 8192)

📈 Decoding Bottleneck and the Flip Technique

  • Decode processes a single token per user sequence, yielding a thin batch dimension M (often M < 64, sometimes M = 1).
  • Matrix A becomes a thin vector (e.g., 1 × 4096), while matrix B (expert weights) remains a large dense block (e.g., 4096 × 8192).
  • Because M is tiny, A cannot fill the hardware’s 64‑row layout, leaving many Tensor Core lanes idle and causing poor utilization.
  • MoE layers fracture the workload across many experts, making them especially sensitive to these constraints.
  • For a topk=8 routine, the effective N dimension inside the fused kernel expands to tens or hundreds of thousands of parameters.
  • Flipping the multiplication (transposing the matrices before PTX assembly) moves the large expert dimension N = 8192 into the first operand position, satisfying the mandatory 64‑row requirement and unlocking hardware prefetching.
  • This re‑alignment matches the exact topography of Hopper silicon, allowing the expansive N dimension to flood the required rows and dramatically improve hardware utilization.

💡 Why It Matters

  • By addressing the structural asymmetry of Hopper’s WGMMA instruction, the fused MoE kernel reduces decode latency.
  • Better utilization of Tensor Core capacity lowers the compute cost of serving MoE‑based LLMs.
  • The technique enables MoE models to retain their capacity‑scaling benefits without incurring prohibitive inference overhead.

item.title: ReplaySSM Restores Fast Decoding for State‑Space Layers in Hybrid LLMs
item.description:
ReplaySSM Restores Fast Decoding for State‑Space Layers in Hybrid LLMs

🔍 Overview

Hybrid large‑language models interleave state‑space model (SSM) layers with a few attention layers. Recent work – ReplaySSM: Cache SSM Inputs, Not State – shows how to make those SSM layers fast again, removing a major latency bottleneck that appears at serving batch sizes.

🧩 How it works

ReplaySSM changes the way an SSM’s internal state is stored during generation:

  • The state is split into a checkpoint (a full copy of the SSM state) and a buffer of recent inputs.
  • Output computation reads only the buffer, while the checkpoint is updated lazily.
  • This separation eliminates three known problems:
    1. State traffic – the full state no longer moves every token.
    2. Rollback for speculative decoding – the buffer can be discarded without reverting a large state.
    3. Error accumulation in a quantized state – rounding errors no longer re‑enter the recurrence each step.

⚙️ Key details

  • Hybrid model examples – NVIDIA Nemotron 3, Qwen 3.5 through 3.8, Kimi‑K3, and GLM‑5.3‑Flash all use this pattern, with Mamba‑2, Gated DeltaNet (GDN), or Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) as the SSM layer.
  • Decoding bottleneck – at batch size 256 on a Blackwell Ultra B300 GPU, SSM layers dominate latency up to 100 K tokens of context (Figure 2, left). The model has five times as many SSM layers as attention layers.
  • State size comparison – one SSM layer’s FP32 state is 4 MiB per sequence, while an FP8 KV entry is 0.5 KiB per token. Thus an SSM state equals an attention KV cache for roughly 8 K tokens.
  • Speculative decoding – a drafter proposes T tokens, the target model verifies them, then rolls back to the last accepted token. Attention rolls back by moving a KV pointer; an SSM’s state has no cheap inverse, so engines store a full snapshot after each draft token. This costs one read and T writes per step and limits how many requests fit in GPU memory, making speculative decoding barely helpful for SSMs.
  • Quantization issue – the quantized state is both the output and the next update’s input, so rounding error recurs at every step.

🚀 Availability

  • The paper is on arXiv and the implementation is on GitHub.
  • ReplaySSM is integrated into NVIDIA TensorRT‑LLM, vLLM, and FlashInfer.
  • Production deployments include GLM‑5.3‑Flash and Kimi‑K3.

💡 Why it matters

By turning the SSM state into a cache of recent inputs rather than a constantly moved full tensor, ReplaySSM restores the speed advantages of attention‑only models for hybrid architectures. This enables existing speed‑up techniques—speculative decoding and low‑precision quantization—to be applied to models that heavily rely on SSM layers, broadening the practical utility of state‑space approaches in large‑scale inference.

Kimi‑K3 KDA

MetaSteer introduces context-aware nonlinear steering for large language models

Researchers propose MetaSteer, a method enabling context-dependent nonlinear steering of large language models via attention-projection adaptations. This approach challenges traditional linear interventions.

💡 Why it matters

MetaSteer addresses information bottlenecks in linear steering methods, offering more flexible context-aware control. Its zero-shot capability demonstrates potential for generalizable alignment across unseen concepts and distributions.

item.title: Accelerating Mixture-of-Experts Training with Amazon EKS, EFA, and DeepEP
item.description:
Accelerating Mixture-of-Experts Training with Amazon EKS, EFA, and DeepEP

AWS has described an architecture optimized to accelerate the training of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, specifically addressing the infrastructure challenges associated with large-scale Reinforcement Learning (RL) post-training.

🔍 Overview

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is a standard architecture for scaling large language models (LLMs) to hundreds of billions or trillions of parameters while maintaining efficient inference through sparsity. However, large-scale RL training—including pipelines based on Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)—places unusual demands on infrastructure. These demands arise because RL combines elastic inference work with tightly coupled model training that requires high-bandwidth communication.

⚙️ Key Details

Large-scale asynchronous RL jobs must optimize two distinct, simultaneous workloads:

  • Rollout Generation: Distributed inference focused on maximizing aggregate throughput rather than minimizing inter-token latency or time to first token (TTFT).
  • Policy Training: Tightly coupled workers that progress in lockstep; any straggling worker or latency spike can trigger NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) timeouts or stall the entire job.

Training MoE models introduces specific constraints compared to dense models. As architectures become more sparse to reduce inference costs, training is constrained more by communication than by compute. A primary source of this overhead is Expert Parallelism (EP), which introduces dynamic all-to-all token routing across devices in addition to standard Tensor Parallelism (TP), Data Parallelism (DP), and Pipeline Parallelism (PP).

🧩 How it works

To address these challenges, an architecture combining the following tools is used:

Component Purpose
Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) Orchestrates large-scale RL training and coordinates heterogeneous compute.
Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) Accelerates large-scale RL training and provides high-bandwidth inter-node communication.
DeepEP Optimizes expert-parallel communication over EFA.

This system must balance three resource constraints to prevent bottlenecks or idle capacity:

  • Accelerator compute
  • Memory (including KV-cache capacity for distributed inference)
  • Network bandwidth

#AWS #MoE #ReinforcementLearning #LLM #Kubernetes

item.description:
Privileged Self-Practice Improves Performance for Multi-Turn LLM Agents

Researchers have introduced Privileged Self-Practice (PSP), a new method for post-training multi-turn LLM agents that addresses the shortcomings of on-policy self-distillation (OPSD).

🔍 Overview

On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) is a popular recipe for post-training agents that supervises a student model at the token level using a stronger teacher view conditioned on privileged information (PI). However, in multi-turn agents, this paradigm can teach the student to act with confidence without the underlying information, leading to performance that falls short of plain RL and, in some cases, below the untrained base model.

🧩 How it works

Privileged Self-Practice (PSP) modifies the use of privileged information by moving it from the loss to the sampler. The process operates as follows:

  • When student rollouts on a task mostly fail, an analyzer model writes a short per-task instruction.
  • This instruction is injected as privileged information in the context.
  • The task is sampled again with the instruction.
  • The model is trained on the result using an unchanged GRPO objective.
  • The privileged information remains in the prompt and never enters the loss.

💡 Why it matters

Verbalized confidence has transitioned from a weak substitute for log-probabilities to a practical soft-scoring mechanism for top-tier models. item.title: EGGROLL and LOO-ROLL Enable Efficient Evolution Strategies for Large Language Models
item.description:
EGGROLL and LOO-ROLL Enable Efficient Evolution Strategies for Large Language Models

EGGROLL introduces low‑rank Gaussian perturbations to make evolution strategies (ES) practical for large language models (LLMs), and LOO‑ROLL refines the estimator to cut variance and improve downstream performance.

🔍 Overview

  • Replaces dense Gaussian weight perturbations with low‑rank Gaussian products (often rank‑one).
  • Rank‑one perturbations occupy a zero‑volume subset of the full matrix space despite having identity covariance.

🧩 How it works

  • The mean EGGROLL update field is derived at finite rank and non‑zero perturbation radii.
  • Population field obtained by applying an explicit resolvent to the gradient of the objective smoothed by the perturbations.
  • The resolvent may introduce a nonconservative component and can reverse local stability of an optimum.
  • EGGROLL remains exact on every quadratic objective regardless of rank or radius.

⚙️ Key details

  • For smooth objectives, the first local finite‑rank correction scales as O(σ²/r); non‑asymptotic bounds control field error under smoothness assumptions.
  • Under a local affine model, rank‑one perturbations increase gradient‑estimator variance by only 2(m+n+1)/(mn+1). For a 4096×4096 matrix this is 0.098 %.
Metric Formula / Value Example (4096×4096)
Variance increase (rank‑one vs dense) 2(m+n+1)/(mn+1) 0.098 %

📊 Results

  • LOO‑ROLL uses a leave‑one‑out estimator, keeping the finite‑rank population field while reducing two antithetic evaluations per direction to one.
  • At equal evaluation cost, LOO‑ROLL halves estimator MSE in transformer blocks.
  • Across ten post‑training settings and models up to 8 B parameters, LOO‑ROLL improves seven outcomes in paired tests, with no significant loss.
  • GSM8K accuracy rises from 38.1 % to 63.0 % at 0.6 B parameters and from 65.9 % to 80.0 % at 8 B parameters.
  • Transformer measurements match the predicted finite‑rank variance; rank‑eight comparisons show no reproducible reward‑based advantage.

💡 Why it matters

  • Enables practical ES for LLMs with far fewer perturbation evaluations.
  • Reduces variance and computational cost while preserving theoretical guarantees.
  • Demonstrates measurable gains on standard benchmarks (GSM8K) for models of various scales.

Source: EGGROLL, Unrolled: Understanding and Improving Low-Rank Evolution Strategies at Scale

item.title: Research Identifies Model-Specific Fragility to Recursive Training Collapse
item.description:
Research Identifies Model-Specific Fragility to Recursive Training Collapse

Researchers have examined how model-generated text returning to training corpora causes output diversity to collapse, discovering that the susceptibility to this degeneration is a property of the individual checkpoint.

🔍 Overview

Using a recursive contamination protocol, researchers allowed 13 publicly released checkpoints to share a common corpus for five generations. The results showed a significant spread in outcomes:

  • Unique 4-gram outcomes ranged from 0.187 to 0.940.
  • Some models remained barely touched, while others degenerated into repetitive fragments.

⚙️ Key details

  • Predictors: Parameter scale alone does not explain collapse, as a three-size ladder within one family is not monotonic in size. Static indicators also failed to predict it.
  • Detection: A model’s fragility in a larger ecosystem can be inferred by letting it iterate on its own output for two or three generations.
  • Consistency: The ordering of model collapse remained stable (Spearman correlation of 0.91–0.98) regardless of random seed or changes to the shared pool composition, including the mixing in of human text.

💡 Why it matters

Collapse speed responds to specific interventions:

  • Top-p tightening: Cutting the low-probability tail at generation time nearly stops collapse within three generations and stabilizes six checkpoints across the spectrum.
  • Data-side filtering: This method slows collapse but does not stop it.

#LLM #MachineLearning #ModelCollapse #AIResearch

Source: A Fragility Spectrum for Recursive Language-Model Training

🧩 Key Features

Haystack 3.0:

  • Transparent architecture for experimentation and deep customization
  • Sandboxed code execution (local/cloud)
  • Massively parallel processing
  • Powers projects like SWE-agent

SWE-ReX:

  • Run commands in shell sessions (local/Docker/AWS/Modal)
  • Support interactive tools (e.g., ipython, gdb)
  • Manage parallel shell sessions
  • Environment-agnostic agent logic
  • Fast parallel execution for benchmarking

⚙️ Technical Details

SWE-ReX allows agents to:

  • Interact with running shell sessions (auto-detect command completion)
  • Use interactive CLI tools in parallel
  • Maintain identical code across execution platforms

💡 Why It Matters

These tools disentangle agent logic from infrastructure, enabling developers to focus on core functionality. SWE-ReX’s parallel execution capabilities streamline large-scale evaluations, while Haystack’s modular design accelerates production deployment of LLM applications.
